text: Scope is locked. Now the first real architecture decision: which tools actually build this. For Riverside, that's SQL Server, SSIS, SSRS, and Power BI — not because they're the only option, but because they fit this budget, this timeline, and this team.

Four real constraints drove it: Riverside already licenses SQL Server, with no cloud budget approved. The freshness target is a nightly batch, not real-time. And there are two very different audiences — fourteen store managers who want one simple page, and one VP who wants to explore across all of them.

Each tool gets exactly one job. SQL Server stores and enforces structure — nothing else. SSIS extracts, cleans, and loads, nightly — no reporting responsibility. SSRS is the single-store, printable report. Power BI is the cross-store, exploratory dashboard. If business logic ever ends up duplicated across two of these, that's the architecture blurring.

We also name what we didn't pick. Azure Data Factory loses to SSIS because there's no cloud budget and SSIS already runs on infrastructure Riverside owns. A single Power BI model for both audiences loses because store managers need a simple printable page, which paginated reporting is built for and a dashboard isn't.
That boundary matters later: when a number looks wrong, we'll know immediately whether to check the SSIS transform logic or a DAX measure — not both, guessing.
With the stack locked, we can finally design the shape of the data itself — the star schema, before opening SQL Server Management Studio even once. That's next.
